details: Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP): 6 × VVER-1000 reactors (1000 MWe each); total capacity 6000 MWe; Europe's largest nuclear power plant; on Kakhovka Reservoir shore of Dnieper River; operated by Energoatom (Ukrainian state nuclear operator); 5400 employees; began operations 1984-1995 (Units 1-6)
safety_assessment: VVER-1000 design: negative void coefficient; containment buildings; fundamentally safer reactor physics than RBMK; see reactor_types_physics_comparison_REAL.csv
source: IAEA Update Report ZNPP 2022-2025; Energoatom; WNA Ukraine

details: Russian armed forces attacked and occupied ZNPP site March 4 2022; fire visible in training building during attack; Ukrainian staff held at gunpoint; first nuclear plant seized in active combat in history; IAEA expressed 'serious concern' immediately; all 6 units under Russian military control
safety_assessment: No reactor damage in initial attack; fire was in training building adjacent to reactor; containment integrity maintained; however all seven IAEA nuclear safety principles subsequently violated according to IAEA report November 2022
source: IAEA Update 11-2022; multiple news sources March 4 2022; NEA/CRPPH/R(2024)3

details: IAEA published report November 2022 stating all 7 principles required for nuclear safety were being violated at ZNPP: (1) physical integrity of structures; (2) functionality of safety/security systems; (3) AC power supply; (4) site logistics; (5) fire protection; (6) radiation monitoring and environmental protection; (7) reliable communications
safety_assessment: Unprecedented: all 7 principles violated simultaneously at an operating nuclear plant; IAEA Director General Grossi personally led multiple missions to ZNPP 2022-2024; permanent IAEA monitoring team stationed on-site
source: IAEA Report NE/ZNPP/2022/3; IAEA Director General Grossi statements Nov 2022

details: External power supply to ZNPP repeatedly severed during fighting: supply line cut multiple times; plant operated on last remaining external 750 kV line on at least 5 separate occasions; reactor safety systems require external power to run pumps for decay heat removal; backup diesel generators available but finite fuel supply
safety_assessment: Loss of ALL external power = station blackout = Fukushima scenario; backup diesels provide ~10-15 days emergency cooling; after that: spent fuel pool temperatures rise → steam/hydrogen → potential release; shelling near high-voltage powerlines created repeated near-misses
source: IAEA Update reports ZNPP 2022-2024; NEA War Impact on Chernobyl report; multiple IAEA situation reports

details: All 6 ZNPP reactors placed in cold shutdown by September 11 2022; decision made by Energoatom to maximize safety margin; Units 1-3 in cold shutdown for maintenance; Units 4-6 initially maintained in warm shutdown for on-site heating water; by late 2022: all units in cold shutdown or hot condition for minimum cooling
safety_assessment: Cold shutdown significantly reduces decay heat load and safety risk; however spent fuel pools still require cooling; 2000+ spent fuel assemblies in on-site spent fuel pools generate ~5-10 MW total decay heat requiring continuous cooling

details: ZNPP spent fuel pools: ~2000+ spent fuel assemblies from prior operations; plus fresh fuel (unirradiated) stored on-site; total radioactive inventory in pools substantial; pool cooling requires electric power; loss of cooling → heating → boiling → exposed fuel → zirconium fire scenario (same concern as Fukushima SFP #4)
safety_assessment: As of 2024: spent fuel pools continuously monitored by IAEA team; cooling systems maintained; no elevated radiation readings near pools; main risk remains power supply reliability
source: IAEA ZNPP monitoring reports 2022-2024; WNA Ukraine

details: Multiple confirmed shelling incidents at or near ZNPP: August 5-6 2022 (shelling near Unit 4 spray pond; nitrogen/oxygen supply lines hit); September 2022 (high-voltage tower hit; 3 units lost external power); November 2022 (shelling near Units 1-4; cooling pond affected); May 2024 (drone attack on Unit 6 dome; external damage but no penetration)
safety_assessment: Each shelling incident raised risk of: (1) direct reactor damage; (2) loss of cooling power; (3) staff injury/evacuation; all incidents so far have not resulted in core damage or significant radioactive release; ZNPP containment buildings robust to conventional weapons
source: IAEA Update reports; Ukrainian government; NEA 2024; GC Human Rights 2023

details: Kakhovka dam breach June 6 2023 (see dnieper_river_contamination_REAL.csv): ZNPP sits on Kakhovka Reservoir; after dam breach reservoir level fell; ZNPP cooling pond (separate; on-site) maintained adequate water level from wells and groundwater; IAEA confirmed no safety threat from dam breach to reactor cooling
safety_assessment: ZNPP has on-site cooling ponds and wells independent of Kakhovka Reservoir; the cooling reserve was assessed sufficient; monitoring intensified after breach; no radiological release associated with dam breach at ZNPP

details: Approximately 5400 Ukrainian Energoatom staff at ZNPP before occupation; some left/evacuated; those remaining work under Russian military presence; IAEA documented concerns about staff coercion; some staff arrested/detained and later released; knowledge continuity concerns as some experienced operators departed
safety_assessment: Staff safety and voluntary departure creates knowledge transfer risk; operating nuclear plant with depleted/stressed workforce is safety concern; IAEA repeatedly called for protection of nuclear staff in conflict zones; IAEA nuclear safety convention obligations
source: IAEA Update reports; Energoatom statements; IAEA Director General Grossi statements

details: IAEA established permanent on-site presence at ZNPP from September 2022; team of 2-3 IAEA experts rotates on-site continuously; monitors: ambient dose rates; reactor parameters; spent fuel status; external power supply; equipment condition; regular reports to IAEA Director General and members
safety_assessment: IAEA monitoring documented in weekly update reports (available publicly); no significant radioactive releases detected by IAEA monitors as of early 2025; highest radiological risk remains external power supply reliability
source: IAEA Update NE/ZNPP series 2022-2025; IAEA Director General weekly updates

details: ZNPP VVER-1000 vs Chernobyl RBMK: VVER = negative void coefficient (self-limiting); full containment building; cannot undergo prompt criticality from void alone; primary risk at ZNPP is spent fuel cooling failure (not reactor criticality); fundamentally different accident scenario than Chernobyl; war-caused loss-of-cooling is more analogous to Fukushima scenario
safety_assessment: A Chernobyl-type explosive criticality at ZNPP is physically impossible (negative void coefficient); primary risk is cooling failure leading to fuel damage and release of fission products; this would be serious but of different character than 1986 Chernobyl prompt criticality

details: As of early 2025: ZNPP remains under Russian military occupation; no transfer of control to Ukrainian or IAEA oversight; IAEA continues on-site monitoring; six reactors in cold/warm shutdown; no commercial electricity generation; site within active conflict zone Zaporizhzhia Oblast
safety_assessment: IAEA Director General Grossi continues calls for demilitarization of ZNPP; establishment of protective zone around plant; both sides have agreed in principle but not implemented; safety concerns remain as long as active conflict near site
source: IAEA DG Report to Board of Governors 2024-2025; NEA Chernobyl 2024 (includes ZNPP context)
